terrain.difficultyNotes: Okemo publishes a three-tier split, so percentExpert is null and the 30% top tier sits in percentAdvanced. Treat that 30% with scepticism: OnTheSnow's independent breakdown of the same mountain is 33/38/21/9, and the trails Okemo rates black are consistently gentler than the same rating elsewhere in Vermont. The resort's own site publishes no snowfall figure, which for a mountain claiming 98% snowmaking coverage is a reasonable thing to be quiet about.

pricing.notes: 2026-27 season. Vail prices day tickets dynamically by date and publishes no fixed window rate, so the ticket fields are null rather than estimated. The season pass figure is the full Epic Pass, which is how a season at Okemo is bought; Vail does not sell an unrestricted Okemo-only pass. The cheaper Epic Local carries holiday restrictions and is not recorded here.

editorial.overview: Okemo grooms better than anyone else in New England and has built an entire resort around that one competence. Ninety-eight percent snowmaking coverage, a fleet of winch cats, and a management culture that treats corduroy as the product means that on a Tuesday morning in January you can ski top-to-bottom on a surface that is genuinely flawless while half of Vermont is scraping ice. If what you want is to make fast, clean, confident turns on perfect groomed snow, Okemo is the best mountain in the region and it is not particularly close. What it does not have is difficulty. The published breakdown claims 30% advanced terrain, and that is generous to the point of fiction - Okemo's black diamonds are short pitches that back off quickly, there is essentially no sustained steep skiing, and the glades are an afterthought. Strong skiers get bored here in a day. Which is fine, because Okemo is not selling itself to them: it sells to families from Connecticut, New York and New Jersey who want a reliable, well-run, low-anxiety mountain three hours from home, and it serves them very well. The Jackson Gore base area added a decade ago is the most functional family base in Vermont. Vail bought the place in 2018 and the prices went the way Vail prices go, but the grooming operation survived the transition intact, which was the only thing that really mattered.
editorial.snowQuality: Okemo's natural snowfall is the weakest of any major Vermont resort - around 120 inches by independent measure, roughly a third of Jay's - and the resort pointedly does not publish a figure of its own. It compensates with the most comprehensive snowmaking system in the state, covering 98% of the terrain, and with grooming discipline that is genuinely exceptional. The result is a surface that is consistent and predictable and almost entirely manufactured. That is a real strength in a bad year, when Okemo will be open top to bottom while natural-snow mountains north of it are running half their terrain. It is a weakness after a thaw-freeze cycle, when 667 acres of manmade base sets up hard and the edges of every trail turn to the blue-white boilerplate that gives southern Vermont its reputation. There is very little untracked snow to be found here at any point in the season.
editorial.crowds: Okemo is the closest big Vermont mountain to the New York and Connecticut corridor, and weekends show it. The Sunburst Six and the Quantum Four back up hard between nine and eleven, the Ludlow base lots fill early, and Route 103 into town is genuinely slow on a Sunday afternoon. Jackson Gore, the second base area, is the reliable escape - its own parking, its own lifts, and consistently lighter traffic than the main village side, though it accesses less of the mountain. Epic added destination visitors without adding lift capacity, which is the same story at every Vail property in the East. The compensations are real: Okemo's lift network is large for its size at 20 lifts, so the queues move, and midweek the mountain is quiet and the grooming is at its best.
editorial.difficulty: Okemo rates soft and everybody who skis elsewhere in Vermont knows it. A black diamond here is a strong blue at Sugarbush or Stowe; the steepest sections on trails like Sel's Choice and Outrage last a few hundred vertical feet before the pitch relaxes. For a nervous intermediate that is genuinely valuable - Okemo is one of the best mountains in New England for building confidence, because you can ski a black diamond and survive it, and the progression from green to blue to black is unusually gradual. For anyone looking for a real challenge, the honest answer is that it is not here, and the mountain is a two-hour drive from Killington where it is. The glades exist and are worth a lap on a rare good snow week, but they are thin and short and not the reason to come.

keyTrails.name: Sel's Choice
keyTrails.note: Okemo's steepest sustained pitch, and 'sustained' is doing some work in that sentence. Genuinely good for a few hundred feet before it mellows.

keyTrails.name: Upper World Cup
keyTrails.note: The signature groomer - wide, consistently pitched, immaculately maintained, and the trail that explains why people who love carving love this mountain.

keyTrails.name: Outrage
keyTrails.note: The other black worth doing, off the Glades Peak side. Steeper than the map suggests and quieter than the main face.

keyTrails.name: Defiance
keyTrails.note: Long intermediate cruiser with enough roll and pitch change to stay interesting for more than one lap.

keyTrails.name: Jackson Gore Express terrain
keyTrails.note: Not one trail but the whole quieter pod - its own base, its own parking, and consistently less traffic than the Ludlow side.

tidbits: Okemo has the largest vertical drop in southern Vermont at 2,200 feet.
Snowmaking covers 98% of the trail area - 654 of 667 acres - which is among the highest coverage of any resort in the East.
Independent records put average natural snowfall around 120 inches, the lowest of any major Vermont resort; Okemo publishes no figure of its own.
Vail Resorts acquired Okemo in 2018 and it is now on the Epic Pass.
Okemo opened on 31 January 1956, after an eleven-inch snowstorm.
